Damsel
DAM-zel
noun
From the Old French dameisele, a diminutive of dame (“lady”), from the Latin domina, “mistress of a house”; hence a young unmarried woman, a maiden, a girl.

Biblical Definition

A damsel is a young unmarried woman — a maiden, a girl not yet given to a husband. The word is the Authorized Version’s ordinary term, and it is never a slight; its root is domina, a lady. Abraham’s servant prayed by the well that the LORD would appoint the damsel who should water his camels, and “the damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her” (Gen 24:16) — Scripture notices her chastity as a thing worth recording, and the marriage of Isaac turned upon it. The word’s highest hour is at a deathbed in Capernaum. The mourners laughed Christ to scorn when He said the damsel was not dead but sleeping; He put them all out, took her by the hand, and said, “Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise” (Mar 5:41). “And straightway the damsel arose, and walked” (Mar 5:42) — twelve years old, and raised by a word, for the Lord of life speaks to the dead as a father wakes a child in the morning. Elsewhere a damsel named Rhoda hears Peter at the gate and, for gladness, forgets to open it (Act 12:13) — and the praying church calls her mad, though she was the only one who believed the prayer answered. From Rebekah at the well to Jairus’s daughter on her bed, the damsels of Scripture are named, guarded by God’s law, and dealt with tenderly by Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

A young unmarried woman; a maiden; a girl. From the Latin domina, a lady — never a term of slight.

DAMSEL, a young woman or girl; a maiden not yet married.

From Old French dameisele, a diminutive of dame, from Latin domina, “lady.”

Rebekah was a damsel very fair to look upon, a virgin (Gen 24:16).

Christ raised the damsel of Jairus with a word: “Damsel, I say unto thee, arise” (Mar 5:41).

Rhoda, a damsel of the praying church, heard Peter at the gate (Act 12:13).

Key Scripture

Gen 24:16 — "And the damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: and she went down to the well, and filled her pitcher, and came up."

Mar 5:41 — "And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise."

Mar 5:42 — "And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; for she was of the age of twelve years. And they were astonished with a great astonishment."

Act 12:13 — "And as Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a damsel came to hearken, named Rhoda."

Modern Corruption

A live corruption: the age has made the maiden a joke and her purity a punchline, where God’s law guarded her, His Word named her, and Christ took her by the hand.

expand to see more

The corruption is a mockery. Damsel survives in modern speech only in a sneer — the damsel in distress, the helpless maiden who wants rescuing — and the sneer is aimed past the word at the thing itself: at maidenhood, at chastity before marriage, at a young woman under her father’s roof and God’s law. The age teaches a girl that her virginity is an embarrassment to be disposed of early and her father’s protection an insult to be escaped. Scripture speaks otherwise and without apology. It records of Rebekah that she was a virgin, neither had any man known her, and it does so because the fact is honourable. Deuteronomy 22 hedges the betrothed damsel about with a law that puts her violator to death and, when she is forced in the field where none could save her, says plainly “unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing.” That is not contempt for women; that is a God who counts them worth defending with the sword of the magistrate.

And see how the Lord Himself handles a damsel. The house was full of noise and professional mourners, and He put them all out; He would not have a twelve-year-old girl raised as a spectacle. He took her by the hand — touching the dead, which no priest would do — and spoke to her in her mother’s Aramaic, Talitha cumi, the homeliest words a child could wake to. Then He commanded that something be given her to eat, because she would be hungry. There is the measure of Christ’s regard for the daughters of men: sovereign power over death, exercised with the tenderness of a father at a bedside. An age that jeers at the damsel has never seen her as her Maker sees her, nor watched her Saviour take her by the hand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a young unmarried woman, a maiden — from the Latin for “lady.”

Damsel — Old French dameisele, a diminutive of dame.

From the Latin domina, “mistress of a house, lady.”

It denotes a young unmarried woman, a maiden, a girl.

Rebekah the damsel was fair to look upon, a virgin (Gen 24:16).

Christ raised Jairus’s damsel with a word (Mar 5:41).

Usage

"The damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin — Scripture records her chastity as honour."

"Talitha cumi — Damsel, I say unto thee, arise: and straightway she arose, and walked."

"A damsel named Rhoda believed the prayer was answered, and the praying church called her mad."
